cards.stem: You are called to the recovery ward to see a patient who had surgery 30 minutes ago. He is gagging and struggling to breathe; SpO₂ is 65%.
prompts: What manoeuvre would you use to correct this situation?
What does this manoeuvre entail?
answer: • The jaw thrust maneuver is used to relieve upper airway obstruction, especially in post-operative or unconscious patients who may have airway collapse due to residual anesthesia, muscle relaxation, or airway obstruction by the tongue.
Steps to Perform the Jaw Thrust Maneuver:
(i) Position the Patient: The patient should be in the supine position on a firm surface.
(ii) Hand Placement: Place both hands on either side of the patient’s head, resting the fingers on the angles of the mandible (jaw).
(iii) Lift the Jaw Forward: Using the index and middle fingers, push the mandible upwards and forward, moving the tongue and soft tissues away from the airway.
(iv) Avoid Neck Extension: This maneuver does not require head tilt, making it safe for patients with suspected cervical spine injuries.
(v) Assess Breathing: Look for improvement in airway patency, oxygenation (SpO₂), and breathing effort.

prompts: List five signs and symptoms following an overdose of the drug on the slide. (5 marks)
answer: Lidocaine overdose can lead to systemic toxicity, primarily affecting the central nervous system (CNS) and cardiovascular system (CVS).
(i) Tingling (Peri-oral paresthesia) and Numbness: early signs affecting the lips, tongue, and extremities.
(ii) Dizziness and Lightheadedness: due to impaired neuronal signaling.
(iii) Seizures: at high toxic levels, lidocaine causes CNS excitation followed by depression.
(iv) Loss of Consciousness and Coma: Severe toxicity leads to CNS depression and unresponsiveness.
(i) Hypotension: Due to vasodilation and myocardial depression.
(ii) Bradycardia or Arrhythmias: Lidocaine affects cardiac conduction, leading to bradycardia, heart block, or ventricular arrhythmias.
(iii) Cardiac Arrest: In severe cases, asystole or cardiovascular collapse may occur.
refs: 1. Miller, R. D., & Cohen, N. H. (2020). Miller’s Anesthesia (9th ed.). Elsevier. Page 1680-1683: (Local anesthetic toxicity, including lidocaine overdose effects).
2. Morgan, G. E., Mikhail, M. S., & Murray, M. J. (2018). Clinical Anesthesiology (6th ed.). McGraw-Hill.Page 234-238: (Lidocaine pharmacology and systemic toxicity).

prompts: What quantity (mL) of the drug on the slide is required to safely perform a local infiltration on a child weighing 30 kg? (3 marks)

answer: 1. Dosage (Lidocaine) = 1% (10 mg/mL). The maximum safe dose of lidocaine without epinephrine for local infiltration is = 2–3 mg/kg. For a 30 kg child, the safe dose range is:
Since 1% lidocaine = 10 mg/mL, the corresponding volume is:
Minimum safe volume: 60 mg ÷ 10 mg/mL = 6 mL
Maximum safe volume: 90 mg ÷ 10 mg/mL = 9 mL Therefore, the safe dose of lidocaine for a 30 kg child is 6–9 mL of 1% lidocaine solution.
2. (i) Central Nervous System (CNS) excitation: Early signs include tinnitus, dizziness, metallic taste, and circumoral numbness.
(ii) Seizures: Higher toxicity levels can cause tonic-clonic seizures due to excessive neuronal excitation.
(iii) Cardiovascular Depression: Includes bradycardia, hypotension, and cardiac arrest due to direct myocardial suppression.
(iv) Respiratory Depression: Can lead to apnea due to brainstem depression at high toxic doses.

cards.stem: You are called to the recovery ward to see a patient who had surgery 30 minutes ago. He is gagging and struggling to breathe; SpO₂ is 65%.
prompts: What manoeuvre would you use to correct this situation?
What does this manoeuvre entail?
answer: • The jaw thrust maneuver is used to relieve upper airway obstruction, especially in post-operative or unconscious patients who may have airway collapse due to residual anesthesia, muscle relaxation, or airway obstruction by the tongue.
Steps to Perform the Jaw Thrust Maneuver:

i. Position the Patient: The patient should be in the supine position on a firm surface. ii. Hand Placement: Place both hands on either side of the patient’s head, resting the fingers on the angles of the mandible (jaw). iii. Lift the Jaw Forward: Using the index and middle fingers, push the mandible upwards and forward, moving the tongue and soft tissues away from the airway. iv. Avoid Neck Extension: This maneuver does not require head tilt, making it safe for patients with suspected cervical spine injuries. v. Assess Breathing: Look for improvement in airway patency, oxygenation (SpO₂), and breathing effort.

answer: 2. Situations where Macintosh Laryngoscope is preferred:
(i) Routine Adult Intubation: Used in most adult patients due to its ease of use and reduced trauma.
(ii) Patients with Normal Airway Anatomy: It is effective in individuals without airway abnormalities.
(iii) Rapid Sequence Intubation (RSI): It is preferred in emergency airway management to facilitate quicker visualization.
(v) Patients at Risk of Dental Injury: It causes less pressure on teeth than the miller blade. Situations where Miller Laryngoscope is preferred:
(i) Neonates and Infants: The epiglottis is larger and more floppy in pediatric patients, requiring direct lifting.
(ii) Difficult Airway with Large Epiglottis: When the epiglottis obstructs the view, direct elevation provides better visualization.
(iii) Patients with Anterior Larynx: It helps in difficult intubation cases where the larynx is more anteriorly positioned.
(iv) Patients with Reduced Mouth Opening: Shorter blade length facilitates easier insertion in limited space.
(v) Obese or Edematous Patients: direct epiglottis control aids intubation in patients with airway swelling or obesity.
• The straight blade requires more force to lift the epiglottis, increasing the risk of dental injury, mucosal lacerations, and lip trauma.
• Particularly problematic in patients with poor dentition or limited mouth opening.
• Direct stimulation of the vagus nerve (via the epiglottis or larynx) can cause reflex bradycardia.
• More common in pediatric patients, especially neonates and infants.
(iii) Airway Edema and Soft Tissue Damage
• Excessive pressure on the tongue and pharyngeal structures can cause soft tissue injury, swelling, and postoperative sore throat.
• May result in difficult extubation due to airway narrowing.
• The straight blade design can make it harder to manipulate in adult patients with normal airway anatomy, leading to prolonged intubation attempts and airway trauma.
• Increased risk of hypoxia and aspiration if intubation is delayed.
(v) Esophageal Intubation and Poor Laryngeal Visualization
• If not properly positioned, the Miller blade can push the endotracheal tube into the esophagus, leading to unrecognized esophageal intubation.
